title: Standard algorithms and lambdas
objectives: Use `std::sort`, `std::accumulate` and lambdas instead of hand-written loops.

screens.title: Sorting by a rule
screens.question: Put the strategies in the order `std::sort` leaves them.

hints.text: The rule returns true when `a` should come first. When does it?
`a.sharpe > b.sharpe`: the larger Sharpe goes first.
Largest Sharpe first: 1.9, 1.4, 1.1, 0.9, 0.6.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The rule puts `a` before `b` when `a` has the larger Sharpe.

explain.text: `std::sort` asks the rule about pairs and arranges the range so that it never says a later element should come first. With `>`, larger Sharpe ratios come first, like `reverse=True`. The bit in `[]() { ... }` is a **lambda**, C++'s `lambda`.

screens.prose: Python's `sum(pnl)` is `std::accumulate(pnl.begin(), pnl.end(), 0.0)` from `<numeric>`. It starts a total at the third argument and adds each element in turn. Slide through the five days of P&L, in pounds.
screens.question: What does `std::accumulate(pnl.begin(), pnl.end(), 0.0)` return?

hints.text: Slide to 5 and read the caption.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide to the end, 5 of 5.

byKey.first: That is only the first day. `accumulate` runs from `begin()` to `end()`, all five days.
byKey.four: That is four days. `end()` is past the last day, so day 4 is added too.

explain.text: `accumulate` is a loop you do not write: start at 0.0, add each element from `begin()` up to `end()`. The iterators say which elements; the third argument says where the total starts and what type it has.

screens.title: A lambda with a capture
screens.question: Tap every return the lambda counts.

hints.text: `std::abs(r)` drops the sign before comparing.
−0.03 has size 0.03, which is above 0.02.

feedback.correct: Three moves bigger than 2% either way.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the size of each return, ignoring its sign, with 0.02.

byKey.pos: You kept the sign. `std::abs(-0.03)` is 0.03, which is above the limit.
byKey.half: You counted −0.005, whose size is 0.005: below 0.02.

explain.text: The lambda sees `limit` because `[limit]` copied it in. `count_if` returns 3: Python's `sum(1 for r in rets if abs(r) > limit)`. `[&limit]` would capture a reference instead, `[=]` copies every local it uses and `[&]` refers to them all.

screens.title: VWAP without a loop
screens.prose: VWAP is the volume-weighted average price: $\sum p_i q_i / \sum q_i$. `std::inner_product(a.begin(), a.end(), b.begin(), 0.0)` multiplies pairs and adds them up. Use `accumulate` for the shares. Return 0 when no shares traded.
screens.question: Write `vwap(px, qty)` with standard algorithms.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB), and the first compile takes 10 to 15 s; later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs 5 hidden tests that call vwap; each answer is accepted within a relative 1e-9 (a zero must be exactly 0).

hints.text: Two totals: the traded value and the shares.
`std::accumulate(qty.begin(), qty.end(), 0.0)` gives the shares. Check it before dividing.
`double shares = accumulate(...)`; if it is 0 return 0; else return `inner_product(px.begin(), px.end(), qty.begin(), 0.0) / shares`.

feedback.correct: Value over volume, in two calls.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-3: No fills means no shares. Return 0 before dividing, or you get 0 / 0, which is NaN.
byKey.test-4: Two fills of 0 shares: the volume is 0, so return 0.
byKey.test-1: Expected 100.75. If you got 101, you averaged the prices without weighting them by shares.

explain.text: `inner_product` walks two ranges in step: `px` from `begin()` and `qty` from its own `begin()`. The `0.0` start makes the totals `double`. Divide only after checking the volume, because `0.0 / 0.0` is NaN.

screens.title: Price, then time
screens.prose: Bids queue by price, then by time: the highest price first and, at one price, the earliest order first. `Order` is supplied with `price`, `qty` and `time`. `b` comes in by value, so sort it and return it.
screens.question: Write `sort_book(b)` with `std::sort` and a lambda.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB), and the first compile takes 10 to 15 s; later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs 5 hidden tests that call sort_book and read prices, sizes or the order of the times; each must match exactly.

hints.text: The lambda gets two orders and returns true when the first should come first.
Compare prices first. Only when they are equal, compare times.
`if (x.price != y.price) return x.price > y.price; return x.time < y.time;`

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: Expected times 9, 2, 4, 7. If 7 came before 2, the tie on price was not broken by time.
byKey.test-4: Six orders at one price. If the program stopped with a strict-weak-ordering message, your rule used `<=` or `>=`: use strict `<` and `>`.
byKey.test-1: The best bid is 100.6. If you got 100.4, the prices sort ascending: use `>` for price.

explain.text: The lambda decides by price and falls back to time only on a tie, like Python's `key=lambda o: (-o.price, o.time)`. The rule must be strict: for two equal orders it returns false both ways. Comparing doubles with `!=` is safe here because prices come from the book unchanged.

screens.title: Up days, again
screens.prose: In lesson 3 you counted up days with a loop. Now use algorithms. `std::adjacent_difference` writes `px[0]`, then `px[1] - px[0]`, `px[2] - px[1]` and so on into a range of the same size. Its first output is not a difference.
screens.question: Write `count_up_days(px)` with `adjacent_difference` and `count_if`.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB), and the first compile takes 10 to 15 s; later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs 6 hidden tests that call count_up_days; each must return exactly the expected count.

hints.text: Make `std::vector<double> d(px.size())` to receive the differences.
Test 4 falls every day, but `d[0]` holds 5.0, which is positive.
Count from `d.begin() + 1`: `std::count_if(d.begin() + 1, d.end(), [](double x) { return x > 0; })`. Return 0 early for fewer than two closes.

feedback.correct: Differences, then a count that skips the first slot.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-4: Three falling closes have no up days. If you got 1, you counted `d[0]`, which is the first close itself: start at `d.begin() + 1`.
byKey.test-2: An empty vector has no days. `d.begin() + 1` on an empty range is past the end, so return 0 first.
byKey.test-1: Expected 2. If you got 3, the first close, 100, was counted as a rise.

explain.text: `adjacent_difference` keeps `px[0]` in slot 0 so the output has the same size; skipping it is the classic slip. Each algorithm names its job, so a reader sees *differences, then count* without tracing a loop.

screens.title: Where transform writes
screens.question: What does `pence` hold afterwards?

options.text: Nothing: its size is still 0, and three values went to memory it does not own

options.why: You expected `transform` to grow `pence`. It only writes where `pence.begin()` points, and an empty vector has no room there.
It compiles: `pence.begin()` is a valid iterator. The compiler cannot see that the range is too short.
Algorithms do not check iterators. Only `at` throws `std::out_of_range`.

hints.text: How many slots does an empty vector have to write into?
`transform` writes three values starting at `pence.begin()`.
There is no room, so the writes are undefined behaviour and `size()` stays 0.

feedback.correct: The writes went nowhere legal; `pence` is still empty.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Does an algorithm ever change a vector's size?

explain.text: Algorithms see only iterators, so they cannot call `push_back`. Pass `std::back_inserter(pence)` from `<iterator>`, an output iterator that calls `push_back` for each write. Or make room first with `pence.resize(px.size())`.

screens.title: The type of the start
screens.prose:
The same five days of P&L, summed with a habit from Python, where `sum` starts at the integer 0.

```cpp
auto total = std::accumulate(pnl.begin(), pnl.end(), 0);
```
screens.question: What is `total`?

hints.text: The third argument sets the type of the running total.
`0` is an `int`. What happens to `0 + 120.5` when it is stored back in an `int`?
Each step truncates: 120, 79, 154, 143, 173.

feedback.correct: 173: every step truncated the total to an `int`.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the running total as an `int` after every addition.

byKey.exact: You summed exactly, as Python would. Here the total is an `int`, so each step drops its fraction: 120, 79, 154, 143, 173.
byKey.trunc: You truncated only once, at the end. The total is an `int` throughout, so every step loses its fraction.

explain.text:
`accumulate` keeps its total in the type of the start value. With `0` that is `int`, so 120.5 becomes 120, then 79.75 becomes 79, and so on. Write `0.0`, and the total is a `double`: 175.

```cpp
std::accumulate(b, e, 0);    // int: 173
std::accumulate(b, e, 0.0);  // double: 175
```

screens.prose:
The algorithms you used, beside their Python.

```cpp
std::sort(b, e, less);          // sorted(xs, key=...)
std::accumulate(b, e, 0.0);     // sum(xs)
std::inner_product(b, e, b2, 0.0);
std::count_if(b, e, pred);      // sum(1 for x if pred(x))
std::transform(b, e, out, f);   // [f(x) for x in xs]
std::max_element(b, e);         // max(xs), as an iterator
std::find_if(b, e, pred);       // first match, or e
std::partial_sum(b, e, out);    // running totals
```
screens.question: `pnl` is empty. What does `std::max_element(pnl.begin(), pnl.end())` return?

options.text: `pnl.end()`, which you must not read through

options.why: There is no element to point at. An empty range has only its end.
Algorithms never throw for an empty range. They return the end iterator.
That would be a value. `max_element` returns an iterator, and here it is `end()`.

hints.text: What can an iterator into an empty range point at?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Where does an empty range begin and end?

explain.text: `max_element` and `find_if` return `end()` when nothing qualifies, so check before `*it`. Reading through `end()` is undefined; this app printed nothing at all when we tried it. Sorting an empty vector, by contrast, is fine: there is nothing to do.

screens.title: Drawdown of a P&L
screens.prose: A desk tracks a strategy's cumulative P&L, which starts at £0. `std::partial_sum` turns daily P&L into running totals. Return the worst fall, in pounds, from the highest total so far, counting the £0 start. A lambda capturing `[&peak, &worst]` can update both as `std::for_each` walks the totals.
screens.question: Write `worst_drawdown(daily)`.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB), and the first compile takes 10 to 15 s; later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs 6 hidden tests that call worst_drawdown; each answer is accepted within a relative 1e-9 (a zero must be exactly 0).

hints.text: First `std::partial_sum(daily.begin(), daily.end(), cum.begin())`.
Start `peak` at 0, the P&L before day 1, so an early loss counts as a drawdown.
`std::for_each(cum.begin(), cum.end(), [&peak, &worst](double c) { peak = std::max(peak, c); worst = std::max(worst, peak - c); });`

feedback.correct: Running totals, then a running peak.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-3: Losing £50 then £30 from a £0 start is a drawdown of £80. If you got 30, your peak started at the first total, −50, not at 0.
byKey.test-1: The totals peak at £120 and fall to −£30: £150. If you got 0, the lambda changed copies: capture with `&`.

explain.text: `partial_sum` gives 120, 70, −30, 50, −10, 190, and the worst fall is from 120 to −30. The lambda must capture by reference: `[peak, worst]` would update copies and return 0. These calls inline, so the compiled code is as fast as the loop you would write by hand.

ideas: Algorithms take a range as two iterators, `begin()` and `end()`, and never change a container's size; `std::back_inserter` grows one for them.
A lambda `[capture](args) { body }` passes a rule: `[x]` copies a local, `[&x]` refers to it, `[=]` and `[&]` do so for every local used.
`accumulate` totals in the type of its start value, so doubles need `0.0`; comparators must be strict, `<` not `<=`.
summary.trap: `std::accumulate(b, e, 0)` on doubles adds in `int` and drops every fraction; start at `0.0`.

quiz.prose:
```cpp
std::sort(px.begin(), px.end(),
    [](double a, double b) { return a <= b; });
```
`px` holds 100.5, 100.5, 99.8.
quiz.question: What is wrong?

options.text: `<=` says each of two equal prices goes first, which breaks `sort`'s rules

options.why: It may look sorted, but for equal prices it answers true both ways. `sort` can then read past the range; this app's library stops it.
`<=` still puts smaller prices first. The problem is the answer for two equal prices.
It compiles. Only running it reveals the broken rule.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. What does the lambda say about two equal prices?

explain.text: For `a == b` a comparator must return false both ways: neither goes first. `<=` returns true both ways, so `sort` may run off the end of the range. Use `<`.

quiz.question: What goes wrong when the returned lambda is called?

options.text: It reads `limit`, which ended when `make_filter` returned

options.why: A reference capture does not keep anything alive. `limit` died with the function's stack frame.
It compiles. The compiler does not track lifetimes across the return.
It reads whatever memory is there now, which is undefined. Capture by value: `[limit]`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. How long does `limit` live?

explain.text: `[&limit]` stores a reference to a local that ends at `return`. Any later call reads freed stack memory. A lambda that outlives its scope must capture by value, `[limit]` or `[=]`.

quiz.prose: Python: `best = sorted(fills, key=lambda f: f.price)[0]`. You want the C++ cheapest fill without sorting the whole vector.
quiz.question: Which call fits?

options.text: `std::min_element(fills.begin(), fills.end(), [](const Fill& a, const Fill& b) { return a.price < b.price; })`

options.why: `accumulate` adds things up. It does not pick an element.
That counts fills with a positive price. It returns a number, not a fill.
`find_if` returns the first fill whose price is non-zero, not the cheapest.

feedback.correct: One pass with the same comparator `sort` would use.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which algorithm returns the smallest element under a rule?

explain.text: `min_element` makes one pass and returns an iterator to the cheapest fill, or `end()` if there are none. It takes the same comparator as `sort`.

quiz.prose: Daily P&L of £50, −£20 and £35 goes through `std::partial_sum` into `cum`.
quiz.question: What is `cum`?

options.why: That is the input. `partial_sum` writes running totals.
`accumulate` returns one total. `partial_sum` writes one total per day.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add up the days so far, one day at a time.

explain.text: `partial_sum` writes 50, then 50 − 20 = 30, then 30 + 35 = 65: the cumulative P&L curve, like Python's `itertools.accumulate`.
